same/recall: A linear recurrence keeps all it knows about the past in its state, h. At every token, it multiplies h by the decay, a, then adds the new input, times b.
same/name: A model like this, with an input, a state carrying the past, and an output read from it, is called a state space model. The state is its whole memory; the state space, every value it can take.
same/fixed: Here a is fixed at zero point six for every token, so each word's weight in the state is a to the power of its age: the older, the fainter, whatever the word.
same/want: But once a full stop ends a sentence, its words could go, while the next sentence's words should hold. That needs a decay set by each token, as an LSTM's forget gate is set by each input.
step/drain: Here is a way to set it. Picture the state draining away as time passes: after one unit of time, e to the minus one is left, about zero point three seven.
step/delta: Now let each token say how much time passes while it is read: its step size, delta, the change in time.
step/a: Over a step of delta, the state shrinks to e to the minus delta of itself. That is the decay: a t equals e to the minus delta t.
step/big: A long step forgets: a step of three leaves e to the minus three, about zero point zero five, and the old state is nearly wiped.
step/small: A short step keeps: a step of zero point one leaves about zero point nine, and the state carries on.
step/range: delta is always positive, so the decay lies between zero and one: it shrinks the state, but never grows it, and never quite wipes it.
step/select: And delta is made from the token itself, by a small learned layer. Each token picks its own step, so the model selects what to keep: a selective state space model.
step/mamba: Albert Gu and Tree Dao built this into their model, Mamba, in 2023. State space models had trailed attention on language, they found, since one decay for every token cannot pick out what to keep.
run/set: Run it on numbers: inputs four, two and six, with steps of one, zero point one and three: decays of zero point three seven, zero point nine and zero point zero five.
run/h1: With b at one, start the state at zero. Step one has nothing to fade, so h one is the input, four.
run/h2: Step two's own decay, zero point nine, fades the four it finds; add two, and h two is five point six.
run/h3: Step three forgets: zero point zero five times five point six is about zero point two eight; add six, and h three is six point two eight, almost all new input.
memory/cache: Now the memory. While generating, a transformer's KV cache grows with every token: at thirty two layers and d of four thousand, four thousand tokens take about two gigabytes.
memory/state: A state space model keeps only its state, updated in place: a summary of the past, where the cache keeps every token whole.
memory/shape: A Mamba layer runs twice d of these recurrences side by side, eight thousand here, each keeping, typically, sixteen numbers: a hundred and twenty eight thousand numbers per layer.
memory/mb: Over thirty two layers, at two bytes each, that is about eight megabytes, at any length.
memory/ratio: Compare one layer of each. The cache holds a key and a value of four thousand numbers for each of four thousand tokens: thirty two million numbers.
memory/times: That is two hundred and fifty times the state. Double the context, and the cache doubles; the state stays the same size.
memory/fast: With no cache to hold, a GPU can serve many more sequences at once: Gu and Dao measured four to five times as many tokens per second as a transformer of similar size.
